United States and World War I (1914-1921)
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: Woodrow Wilson, Proclamation of Neutrality, August 4, 1914

stimulus.text:
President Woodrow Wilson, Proclamation of Neutrality, August 4, 1914 (verbatim excerpts):

"Whereas the laws and treaties of the United States, without interfering with the free expression of opinion and sympathy, or with the commercial manufacture or sale of arms or munitions of war, nevertheless impose upon all persons who may be within their territory and jurisdiction the duty of an impartial neutrality during the existence of the contest; . . . Now, Therefore, I, Woodrow Wilson, President of the United States of America, in order to preserve the neutrality of the United States . . . do hereby declare and proclaim . . . That the statutes and the treaties of the United States and the law of nations alike require that no person, within the territory and jurisdiction of the United States, shall take part, directly or indirectly, in the said wars, but shall remain at peace with all of the said belligerents, and shall maintain a strict and impartial neutrality . . ."
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpts from Woodrow Wilson, Proclamation of Neutrality, August 4, 1914 (public domain).

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Woodrow Wilson, Proclamation of Neutrality, August 4, 1914
stem: Which of the following best explains why Wilson's call for strict neutrality became hard for the United States to keep?

options.text: American banks refused to lend money to any warring nation
options.misconception: Background from the books: American banks lent heavily to the Allies, which tied the United States to their side.

options.text: German Americans demanded that the United States join the Central Powers
options.misconception: Background from the books: German Americans were divided, and no large movement demanded joining the Central Powers.

options.text: Britain blockaded American ports on the Atlantic coast
options.misconception: Background from the books: Britain blockaded Germany, not American ports; American ships were stopped and searched, not blockaded at home.

options.text: American trade and loans tied the United States to the Allied economies

rationales.A: Background from the books: American banks lent heavily to the Allies, which tied the United States to their side.
rationales.B: Background from the books: German Americans were divided, and no large movement demanded joining the Central Powers.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Britain blockaded Germany, not American ports; American ships were stopped and searched, not blockaded at home.
rationales.D: The United States sold far more to the Allies than to Germany and lent the Allies large sums. Those ties made true impartiality hard to keep.
rationales.general:
1. Read what neutrality needs: equal treatment of every warring nation.
2. Ask what American trade actually did. It flowed to the Allies, and American loans followed it.
3. See the clash. A nation cannot stay impartial while its money and goods favor one side.
Remember: follow the trade and the loans to see which side a neutral nation is really tied to.
